chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Jameel ibn Salih, from Suleiman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding

a man who employed a wet-nurse, so she disappeared with his son for years. Then she came with him, but his mother denied him, and her family claimed that they do not recognize him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is nothing upon her. The wet-nurse is trustworthy.'
ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on a wet-nurse who disappears with a child for years and returns?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of 'trustworthiness' (amāna) for wet-nurses, ruling that their testimony regarding the child's identity is sufficient without needing corroborating proof from the mother or family. Historically, this reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on preserving the milk-kinship (radāʿ) bond and protecting the nurse's status in a pre-modern context where child abduction or displacement was a significant social concern. It underscores the reliability of the wet-nurse as a primary witness in matters of lineage and custody.

en.hubeali: Ibn Mahboub, from Jameel Bin Salih, from Suleyman Bin Khalid,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> regarding a man who employed a wet-nurse. So she disappeared with his son for years. Then she came over with him, but his mother denied him and her family claimed that they do not recognise him. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is nothing upon her. The wet-nurse has to be trusted’.
en.sarwar: 2. Ibn Mahbub has narrated from Jamil ibn Salih from Sulayman ibn Khalid who has said the following: “About

the case of a man who hires a breastfeeding woman, who disappears with the child for many years, but then she brings the child to his family but the mother refuses to accept the child. The family thinks that they do not know him. He (the Imam) said, ‘She is not responsible for anything; the breastfeeding woman is not liable.’”
